questions.q: What do the ~ and ~* operators do in PostgreSQL?
options: Case-sensitive and case-insensitive regular-expression matching, respectively
String concatenation and repetition
Bitwise AND and OR operations on integers
Array containment and overlap testing
questions.explain: ~ is case-sensitive regex matching, ~* is case-insensitive -- a direct inline regex capability T-SQL doesn't have without CLR workarounds.

questions.q: What makes ILIKE genuinely distinctive compared to SQL Server, Oracle, and MySQL?
options: None of those platforms have a directly equivalent built-in case-insensitive LIKE operator
ILIKE only works on numeric columns
ILIKE is actually identical to LIKE on every platform including PostgreSQL
ILIKE is slower than LIKE on every platform, including PostgreSQL
questions.explain: T-SQL relies on collation settings for case sensitivity, not a direct operator; ILIKE is PostgreSQL's dedicated built-in.

questions.q: What does DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY customer_id, order_date DESC return?
options: One row per customer_id value — specifically the first row per group according to the ORDER BY
Every row, with duplicates removed only when ALL columns match
A count of distinct customer_id values, not the rows themselves
An error, because DISTINCT ON requires no ORDER BY
questions.explain: DISTINCT ON picks exactly one row per distinct value of the given column(s), the first one per the supplied ORDER BY.

questions.q: What would you need to write in T-SQL to get the same result as a PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON query?
options: A CROSS APPLY with no filtering logic needed
Nothing extra — T-SQL's DISTINCT ON works identically
A ROW_NUMBER() window function partitioned by the grouping column, filtered to rn = 1
T-SQL cannot produce this result under any approach
questions.explain: This is the lesson's key comparison: DISTINCT ON replaces what otherwise requires a window function plus a filtering subquery or CTE.

questions.q: Is DISTINCT ON a standard SQL feature available on every platform in this course?
options: Yes — T-SQL has supported DISTINCT ON since SQL Server 2016
No — it's a well-known PostgreSQL-only idiom with no direct equivalent elsewhere
Yes — MySQL has an identical DISTINCT ON clause
Yes — it's part of the ANSI/ISO SQL standard
questions.explain: DISTINCT ON is specifically called out as a PostgreSQL-only convenience, not a standard or widely-ported feature.
